{=BaPDTrWa}No matter how much we adopt modern technology, war must not change. We are samurai, and we shall fight like it.

{=8FARrN5C}Kansai is the centermost region of Japan, and the origin of most strife in the Bakumatsu. Here sonno-joi radicals and shogunate loyalists clash in the streets of Kyoto and in the court of the Emperor. From here arose Tokugawa Iemochi, the current Shogun, and Ii Naosuke, the Tairo who dominated the Bakufu throughout the period until his assassination in 1860. The domains of Kansai were once some of the strongest for the Shogun, but many are being pushed away by their political rivals, forcing them into joining the Imperial cause.

{=37mpLUZE}Tōhoku, the northernmost region of Honshū, was the home of the last holdouts of the Shogunate cause in the Boshin war. The domains here are some of the oldest and most entrenched in Japan, with clans such as the Date of Sendai, the Nanbu of Morioka, and the Tsugaru of Hirosaki having ruled in the same region for centuries. Tōhoku, due to its isolation, is also fairly conservative. Few domains have truly begun reforming, leaving them far behind the rapidly modernizing domains of the southwest.

{=Vybsd8CE}Shikoku maintains a more cautious stance than the rest of Japan. With very few large domains, the island is almost entirely dominated by the Yamauchi of Tosa and the Hachisuka of Tokushima, as well as the Date of Uwajima, a cousin of the larger main house in Sendai. Even so, these few domains are tiny compared to some of the mighty domains in the rest of Japan. The samurai of Shikoku have flocked to the sonno-joi cause en masse, much to the dismay of the more pro-Shogunate daimyo of their domains, and internal conflicts have begun to tear them apart.

{=nIcaL3N3}Kyūshū is the core of Japan's reform in the Bakumatsu. Due to its isolation at the southwest of Japan, the island remained largely untouched by the Tokugawa when they founded the Bakufu, leaving the island largely under the control of powerful tozama daimyo, like the Shimazu of Satsuma, the Nabeshima of Saga, and the Hosokawa of Kumamoto. As the Shogun's authority continues to wane, the daimyo of Kyūshū have seen their chance, rapidly rearming with modern weapons in the hopes of becoming the dominant power in this new era.

{=Tv1hioxg}Chūgoku, stretching across western Honshū, has become one of the most unstable regions of Japan in the Bakumatsu. Once a stronghold of loyalist domains guarding the western approaches to the capital, the region is now defined by upheaval and rebellion, chiefly in Chōshū, whose radical samurai and reformist leadership openly defy the Bakufu, clashing repeatedly with shogunate forces and other loyal domains. Neighboring territories such as Hiroshima and Okayama have been drawn into the turmoil, and Chūgoku is becoming the spark that will light the fire of war.

{=3i4huJOq}Kantō is the heart of the Shogunate. Within it is Edo, the capital of the Bakufu, and in which all daimyo were required to live in off years until 1862. Despite that, the region is not as stable as the Shogun wishes it to be. The samurai of Mito, ruled by one of the chief branches of the Tokugawa, are fierce advocates of expelling the foreign barbarians, a stance that the Shogunate is unable to take, leading to constant agitation and the ongoing Mito rebellion. Even so, the region remains loyal to the Tokugawa, with even the Mito samurai wishing to reform, rather than overthrow the Shogunate.

{=lrQiE8yv}Tōkai, stretching along the southern coast, is the home of the Tōkaidō, the most important of the Five Routes that link Edo to the rest of central Honshū. The Tōkaidō specifically links Edo and Kyoto, and is vital for maintaining the Shogun's control of the Imperial Court. Tōkai is almost entirely Tenryō land, alongside a handful of smaller Fudai domains, with the sole large domain being the Tokugawa branch in Owari. These domains largely remain loyal to the Shogun, but will be some of the first to roll over against the Imperial forces when they marched to Edo.

{=rNXMKhtE}Tōsan, the mountainous heart of central Japan, is highly conservative. Made up almost entirely of Tenryō land and a handful of Fudai daimyo, Tōsan has no great lords of their own, leading to their growing irrelavance in this period, as the powerful daimyo in the fringes of Japan increasingly dominate politics. Even so, Tōsan is vital to the Shogunate's continued dominance, providing a great deal of their manpower and influence.

{=zMOC9gh6}Hokuriku, along the northern coast of Honshū, is one of the most prosperous regions of Japan. Home to some of the wealthiest domains in Japan, especially the Maeda of Kaga, the single wealthiest domain in all of Japan, Hokuriku produces a great deal of the rice used to feed central Honshū. Hokuriku is almost entirely loyal to the Shogunate, with most domains either staying loyal throughout the future Boshin War or refusing to take side. However, their reluctance to reform has placed the domains of Hokuriku in the backseat, becoming less relevant than the poorer but more fiery domains in the southwest and north.

{=zMOC9gh6}Ezo (modern Hokkaidō), home to the Ainu, remained a remote frontier. In the late Bakumatsu, the Matsumae Domain managed small garrisons and fortified trading posts to assert shogunate influence, while Ainu communities maintained autonomous governance. The region was a delicate frontier where indigenous autonomy, limited shogunate oversight, and foreign concerns, particularly Russian encroachment, intersected.

{=Ol9J0wU3}The Tozama are 'outside' lords who, although they submit to the Tokugawa after the decisive battles that establish shogunal supremacy, maintain control over large, semi-autonomous domains and wield considerable local power, wealth, and military strength, yet their political influence within the inner councils of the shogunate remains limited, forcing them to act cautiously and independently in matters of national importance. Their position allows them to preserve strong local authority and maintain sizable, loyal armies, making them capable of both defending their interests and exerting pressure when opportunities arise, but always under the shadow of Tokugawa oversight and exclusion from key decision-making.

{=kraPcdwy}The Fudai are hereditary vassals of the Tokugawa who enjoy long-standing trust and occupy critical administrative and military roles within the shogunate, overseeing strategically located domains that, while often smaller in size, provide essential political and military leverage to maintain the Tokugawa order; their loyalty is relied upon to enforce shogunal policies and manage affairs across the country, giving them consistent access to influence and power, yet they remain tightly constrained by the carefully maintained balance of authority that the shogunate imposes to prevent any one ally from becoming too dominant.

{=TonPcdwy}Tosa dominates southern Shikoku, a land of steep mountains and sheltered valleys that have allowed the Yamauchi clan to cultivate a tradition of independence. The domain produces politically active samurai and reformist thinkers, who travel to Kyoto and Edo to debate modernization and imperial loyalty. Rivers carry lumber and silk to coastal ports, linking the inland valleys to trade networks. When disputes flare between coastal and inland powers, Tosa's samurai are quick to act, using both diplomacy and force to advance the clan's interests.

{=kc0qT7Mo}Spread across river valleys and rugged hills, Morioka has been the seat of the Nanbu clan for centuries. The domain's winters are harsh, but its villages and fortified towns reflect careful planning and resilience. Morioka's samurai maintain long-standing martial traditions, while the local economy depends on a mix of agriculture and horse breeding. Centuries of governance have forged a community where survival and endurance shape both politics and everyday life.

{=HurqT7Hi}Hirosaki, perched near the northern tip of Honshu, is defined as much by its rivalry with Morioka as by its own lands. The Tsugaru clan governs fertile plains crossed by rivers, supporting villages and castle towns that thrive despite the harsh climate. Its samurai are fewer than Morioka's but disciplined, and the domain often shifts alliances to avoid being dominated by neighbors. Festivals, shrines, and the rhythms of local life give Hirosaki a cultural identity distinct from its northern rivals.

{=kc0qT7Ak}Kubota stretches across the northern plains toward the Sea of Japan, where the Satake clan balances tradition with pragmatism. Its winters are bitter, but the land yields rice and supports horse breeding, sustaining both townspeople and samurai. The domain is famous for retaining the old ways: its warriors are said to be the last in Japan to fight fully armored. Though deeply conservative, Kubota leans toward the imperial cause, guided by practical concerns rather than ideology, blending old martial habits with careful political calculation.

{=kc0qT7Sh}Shonai occupies a long strip along the Sea of Japan, where fertile farmland and maritime trade enrich the Sakai clan. Unlike many northern neighbors, Shonai adapts quickly, modernizing weapons and training without abandoning its traditions. Its castle towns hum with commerce, and local craftsmanship flourishes alongside the growing military reforms. The domain's leaders remain deeply loyal to the shogunate, yet their readiness and organization make Shonai one of the most capable forces in the north.

{=SendT7ks}Sprawling across southern Tōhoku, Sendai has been shaped over generations by the Date clan. Rivers, plains, and rolling hills support large towns and productive farms, while fortified castles reflect the clan's long martial history. Sendai's culture values practical governance and education, and samurai numbers are substantial. Politically, the domain remains loyal to the shogunate, but the leadership watches events in the southwest closely, balancing caution with preparation for change.

{=kc0qT7Yo}Yonezawa is a smaller, mountainous domain under the Uesugi clan, with a history of careful stewardship after past losses. Its towns cling to hillsides and valleys, sustaining a tight-knit community of farmers and samurai. Local culture emphasizes tradition, efficiency, and scholarly pursuits, and the samurai are respected as much for their administrative skill as for martial ability. Politically, Yonezawa treads carefully, maintaining loyalty while watching the ambitions of larger neighbors.

{=kc0qT7Ai}Nestled in the mountains of southern Tōhoku, Aizu has long been a fortress of the Tokugawa. Its river valleys support fertile rice fields, while dense forests provide timber and fuel for the region's castles and towns. Generations of Matsudaira rulers shaped the domain into a stronghold of martial tradition, where warriors trained from youth and the people prized honor and duty. Temples, local crafts, and educational institutions thrive alongside military life, giving Aizu a culture both disciplined and deeply rooted in centuries of history.

Its river valleys support fertile rice fields, while dense forests provide timber and fuel for the region's castles and towns. Generations of Matsudaira rulers shaped the domain into a stronghold of martial tradition, where warriors trained from youth and the people prized honor and duty. Temples, local crafts, and educational institutions thrive alongside military life, giving Aizu a culture both disciplined and deeply rooted in centuries of history.

{=Ozu7C2Ky}Ozu sits on the western coast of Shikoku, where rocky shores and sheltered bays shape both life and defense. The Katō clan governs a domain where fishing, salt production, and local trade sustain towns and samurai alike. Its castle overlooks the sea, a reminder of past conflicts and the domain's reliance on maritime knowledge. Ozu values prudence and order, blending coastal commerce with disciplined administration to maintain stability in a small but tightly organized domain.

{=Da97CIwo}Iwo-Matsuyama, ruled by the Matsudaira clan, occupies a coastal and mountainous region of Shikoku, where fertile river valleys meet rocky hills. Its towns are modest but well-organized, with local markets supporting both farmers and samurai households. The domain has a long history of managing these challenging lands, emphasizing careful administration and fortification rather than sheer military strength. While its samurai maintain traditional martial training, the domain also leans on commerce, fishing, and regional trade to sustain its people.

{=Da97CUwa}Uwajima domain is led by a branch of the Date clan, located far from their homeland in Sendai. During the Bakumatsu period, their Daimyo, Date Munenari, was considered one of the Four Wise Lords of the Bakumatsu, alongside Yamauchi Toyoshige, Shimazu Nariakira, and Matsudaira Yoshinaga. During the Bakumatsu, they remained neutral, acting as a go between between the two sides, a stance which ultimately left them less relevant in the Meiji era.

{=Da97CTok}Tokushima Domain, despite their strong connections to the Shogunate, remained neutral during the Bakumatsu. Instead of supporting the Shogun or Emperor, they advocated for the kōbu gattai movement, which proposed the unification of the Imperial court and Shogunate against the western powers. Even so, many Tokushima samurai were rather radically pro-Imperial.

{=c1iM3mw8}The capital in name of Japan, Kyoto is the seat of the Emperor. Once the power center of Japan, its decline during the late Sengoku period and throughout the Edo period have left the city a shell of its former self. However, the turmoil of the Bakumatsu has brought the city back to relevance, as Daimyo clash in the halls of government and samurai and ronin clash in the streets of the city.

{=2FMOGwHi}Hikone sits along the shores of Lake Biwa, dominated by its sprawling castle and the Ii clan, whose samurai are famous for their bright red armor and fierce discipline. The Ii have long been loyal to the Tokugawa, serving as both military leaders and administrators of the shogunate. The assassination of Ii Naosuke sent shockwaves through the domain, and his retainers seethe with outrage against the Sonno-joi movement.

{=2FMOGwKu}Ruled by the Hisamatsu Matsudaira, the Kuwana domain is fiercely loyal to the Shogunate, with members of the domain fighting through the end of the war in the North and in Ezo. During the war, their soldiers will be some of the best trained and drilled among all the Shogunate troops.

{=2FMOGKis}Kishu, alternatively named Kii or Wakayama, is a powerful shinpan domain and the fifth richest domain in Japan. It is ruled by one of the three Gosanke houses, descendants of Tokugawa Ieyasu who exist as backups in case the main Tokugawa line ever falters. Despite providing the current Shogun, Iemochi, Kishu domain will go on to surrender to and join the Imperial side

{=2FMOGTsu}Rising out of humble roots, Tsu domain was founded by Todo Takatora, a low ranking ashigaru who later became a daimyo under Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Oda Nobunaga. Due to their loyalty to the Shogunate, samurai in the Edo period often state that 'If the battle occurs, the vanguard is the Hikone's Ii clan and the Todo clan of Ise.'

{=vNsphaFu}The location of the main branch of the Yuki Matsudaira, Fukui-han is a wealthy modernized domain. In the 1850s, they instituted one of the first vaccination programs in Japan, and they've modernized their military, phasing out their archery corps in favor of riflemen. Their lord had an eye for talent, with statesmen like Yokoi Shōnan, Hashimoto Sanai and Yuri Kimimasa rising out of Fukui.

{=vNsphNga}Nagaoka is far more modernized than most Shogunate domains, reforming under the leadership of Kawai Tsugunosuke. Nagaoka is the rare exception to the northern refusal to modernize, being one of the few domains in Hokuriku and Tohoku to fully modernize, at one point owning 2/3 of the Gatling Guns in Japan.

{=vNsphKag}Kaga Domain stretches across Hokuriku, a land of fertile plains, bustling towns, and the glittering rivers that feed into the Sea of Japan. The Maeda clan has ruled for generations, amassing wealth that rivals even the shogunate in scale, and even their lesser retainers are as wealthy as Daimyo. However, Kaga is also deeply unwilling to reform, for fear of being targetted by the Shogunate.

{=vNsphOba}Obama Domain hugs the northern coast of Wakasa Bay, where the town's harbor has long connected the mountains to the sea. The Sakai clan rules here with a careful hand, balancing the needs of merchants, fishermen, and samurai. The domain is known for its skilled boatmen and fortified castle that watches over both river traffic and coastal approaches.

{=y6BfVJoz}A fairly new and small domain, Jozai is highly loyal to the Shogunate. They would fight throughout the entire war, only surrendering upon hearing that the Shogun would keep a fief after the war. Jozai was one of only two domains to be stripped of their holdings during the Boshin war.

{=y6BfVOwa}Owari is ruled by the seniormost of the Gosanke of the Tokugawa. Owari-han is a powerful and wealthy domain, behind only the Kaga, Satsuma, and Sendai domains, and the most powerful of the Tokugawa houses besides the Shogunate itself. Despite their family ties, however, Owari would go on to support the Imperial forces during the Boshin War.

{=y6BfVMit}Despite being ruled by one of the Gosanke of the Tokugawa, Mito Domain is a hotbed of Sonno-joi and anti-Shogunate sentiment in the Bakumatsu. Throughout this period, agitators from Mito constantly undermine the Shogunate and push other domains to adopt the ideology. While not as influential as Satsuma and Choshu would come to be, it cannot be denied that Mito was one of the cores of the Sonno-joi.

While not as influential as Satsuma and Choshu would come to be, it cannot be denied that Mito was one of the cores of the Sonno-joi.

{=y6BfVTen}The Tokugawa may be the Shoguns, but they are also daimyo. At its core, the Bakufu is simply a domain so powerful that all others must bow to it. This power is maintained via Tenryo, land directly under the control of the Tokugawa. Containing some of the wealthiest cities and areas of Japan, most of Tokai, Tosan, and Kanto was Tenryo, as was significant chunks of Kyushu, Chugoku, and Kansai.

{=y6BfVEdo}No city in Japan is greater than Edo, the seat of the Shogunate. From here reign the Tokugawa shoguns, and it is here that over one million people live in the peace that is the Edo period. The center of Japan in many ways, Edo is the center of culture, administration, the economy, and the military. The influence it had upon Japan in this period cannot be overstated, and it is here that the deals and alliances that led to the fall of the Bakufu were formed.

This power is maintained via Tenryo, land directly under the control of the Tokugawa. Containing some of the wealthiest cities and areas of Japan, most of Tokai, Tosan, and Kanto was Tenryo, as was significant chunks of Kyushu, Chugoku, and Kansai.

{=OOBz6Cho}Chōshū occupies the western tip of Honshu, with rugged mountains and jagged coasts that have long shaped the character of its people. The Mōri clan has ruled here for generations, cultivating a culture of fierce independence and hatred of the Shogunate. Samurai from Chōshū are known for their sharp swords, quick thinking, and readiness to defy authority when necessary. In recent years, Choshu has emerged as a hotbed of political action, containing many of the most radical ishin shishi in Japan.

The Mōri clan has ruled here for generations, cultivating a culture of fierce independence and hatred of the Shogunate. Samurai from Chōshū are known for their sharp swords, quick thinking, and readiness to defy authority when necessary. In recent years, Choshu has emerged as a hotbed of political action, containing many of the most radical ishin shishi in Japan.

{=OOBz6Hir}Hiroshima Domain sprawls across the fertile delta of the Ota River, with the castle town at its center serving as both administrative hub and cultural heart. The Asano clan has ruled here for generations, known for disciplined samurai and a stable, well-organized administration. The domain has long fostered artisans, merchants, and schools, giving it a reputation for both martial and cultural refinement. Politically, Hiroshima maintains a careful balance: its samurai enforce order and support the shogunate when called upon, but the radicals of Choshu force them further towards the sonno-joi side.

{=Totz6uxY}Tottori-han, ruled by the Ikeda, has long been close with the Shogunate. Their daimyo are allowed to use the Matsudaira name and crest, they have the right to carry their swords into Edo castle, and their daimyo is the half brother of the man who will one day become the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu. However, they also have many proponents of the Imperial cause within, and just the year ago a pro-Imperial samurai assassinated a pro-Shogunate official within their domain.

{=OOBz6uOk}One of the few Tozama daimyo to serve under the Shogunate, the Ikeda of Okayama domain are relatively sonno-joi, but still support the Shogunate. During the Boshin War, seeing the threat, the daimyo adopted a more pro-imperial successor and retired, so as to allow the domain to take the winning side without violating his own beliefs. While the domain itself avoided joining the war, many units formed in the domain would go fight in the north.

{=BTSZWKur}Kurume domain is a fierce battleground between Sonno-Joi and Shogunate supporters, both originating from the Tenpo School. Following the death of Arima Yorinaga in 1846, they split into the Gai-doshi, a radical sonno-joi traditionalist faction, and Nai-doshi, a reformer, pro-western, pro-shogunate factions. Currently, the Nai-doshi hold sway, but who knows if that will change.

{=BTSZWKum}One of the wealthiest domains in Japan, Kumamoto is ruled by the Hosokawa clan, one of the most powerful clans in Japan. They are more hesitant to join the Emperor than many of the more radical domains, but are still a powerful modern domain.

{=BTSZWHit}Nestled in the valleys of southern Kyushu, Hitoyoshi is a small but proud domain, its hills and rivers shaping life as much as the Sagara clan that rules it. Their samurai, like so many others in the period, are deeply split between the Shogunate and Emperor, leading to their own internal clashes.

{=BTSZFuku}Fukuoka is very prominently Sonno-joi, so much so that the Shogunate is considering arresting their daimyo on suspicion of rebellion. However, they are unwilling to actually dedicate their own troops to the cause, instead using forces they consider expendable, cobbled together from what the dregs of society to war against the Shogunate.

{=BTSZWkKo}Kokura is the rare Shogunate loyalist in the southwest, supporting the Shogun even despite being surrounded by larger, more pro-Imperial domains. This attitude remains ever despite losses against the sonno-joi forces, an almost admirable attitude if it didn't end up with a burning castle.

{=BTSZWSaga}Saga is perhaps the most modern domain in Japan. The Nabeshima have invested in steam engines, steel refining, artillery, and modern firearms, alongside vaccination programs and significant domain reforms, modernizing even before the Black Ships arrived in 1853. There are few domains friendlier to the west than Saga.

{=BTSZWSat}Satsuma occupies a unique position in the late Bakumatsu. The Shimazu joined the shogunate under their own terms due to their distance from the rest of Japan and their military power, providing them with a semi-independent status. The domain is highly militarized, with more samurai than any other domain in Japan, and samurai renowned for their loyalty, identifying first as Satsuma men before anything else. They are also rapidly reforming, forming some of the most modern troops in Japan.
